title: Carcinoma In Situ: Pathology and Clinical Relevance
subject: Pathology
summary: Carcinoma in situ (CIS) represents abnormal cell growth confined to the epithelial layer, not yet invading the basement membrane. It is a pre-invasive form of cancer with the potential to progress to invasive carcinoma if left untreated. Early detection and management are crucial for preventing metastasis.

sections.p: Carcinoma in situ (CIS) refers to a group of abnormal cells that are confined to the epithelial layer where they originated and have not invaded deeper tissues by breaching the basement membrane. This means they cannot metastasize. Diagnosis is primarily made through histopathological examination of a biopsy specimen, identifying characteristic cellular atypia and architectural distortion without evidence of invasion.
b: Abnormal cell changes are confined to the epithelial layer.
Basement membrane remains intact, preventing metastasis.
Histopathological examination is essential for definitive diagnosis.
Examples include Ductal Carcinoma In Situ (DCIS) of the breast and Squamous Cell Carcinoma In Situ (SCCIS) of the skin or cervix.

sections.p: CIS is considered the highest grade of pre-invasive neoplasia. It is not staged using the TNM system, as that system applies to invasive cancers. Instead, its severity is described by its presence and extent. For breast cancer, DCIS is often graded as low, intermediate, or high, reflecting the degree of cellular atypia and necrosis. Lobular Carcinoma In Situ (LCIS) is considered a marker of increased risk for invasive cancer rather than a direct precursor.
b: CIS is not staged by the TNM system.
Severity is described by extent and histological grade (e.g., low, intermediate, high for DCIS).
Untreated low-grade DCIS progresses to invasive cancer at approximately 1% per year.
LCIS is a risk indicator, not a direct precursor to invasive cancer.

sections.p: The development of carcinoma in situ is multifactorial, involving genetic mutations, environmental exposures, and chronic inflammation. Clonal expansion of mutated epithelial cells is a fundamental step. Specific risk factors vary depending on the site.
b: Chronic exposure to carcinogens (e.g., tobacco smoke for bronchial CIS, UV radiation for skin SCCIS).
Human Papillomavirus (HPV) infection is a major cause of cervical and anogenital CIS.
Genetic predispositions and family history play a role in some cases (e.g., breast CIS).
Immunosuppression (e.g., HIV infection) increases the risk of various CIS types.
Cryptorchidism and hypospadias are risk factors for testicular carcinoma in situ.

sections.p: Carcinoma in situ is often asymptomatic and discovered incidentally during screening or investigation for other conditions. When symptoms do occur, they are typically non-specific and depend on the affected organ.
b: Cervical CIS: Often asymptomatic, detected by Pap smear.
Breast DCIS: May present as a mammographic abnormality (microcalcifications) or rarely a palpable mass.
Skin SCCIS (Bowen's disease): Persistent red, scaly patch or plaque, often on sun-exposed areas.
Erythroplasia of Queyrat (SCCIS of glans/prepuce): Velvety bright red plaques, almost exclusively in uncircumcised men.
Zoon's balanitis (resembles CIS): Well-defined red, flat lesion with 'cayenne pepper' spots on glans/prepuce.

sections.p: Investigations aim to detect the lesion, confirm the diagnosis, and rule out invasion. The choice of investigation depends on the suspected site.

t.b: To obtain tissue for histopathological examination and confirm the diagnosis of CIS, distinguishing it from invasive cancer or benign conditions. A positive result shows atypical cells confined to the epithelium without basement membrane invasion.
To screen for breast abnormalities like microcalcifications, which can indicate DCIS. Microcalcifications may suggest DCIS, prompting further investigation.

To screen for abnormal cervical cells, indicating potential cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) or CIS. Abnormal cells (e.g., high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion - HSIL) require colposcopy and biopsy.
To visualize the cervix and guide biopsies of suspicious areas identified by Pap smear. Biopsy confirms the presence and grade of CIN or CIS.
To identify underlying immunosuppression that may increase the risk or alter the course of CIS. A positive result indicates the need for co-management of HIV.

sections.p: The primary red flag for carcinoma in situ is its potential to progress to invasive cancer if untreated. Complications arise from this progression and the impact of treatment.
b: Progression to invasive carcinoma is the most significant complication.
Local recurrence after treatment, especially if margins are not clear.
Psychological distress from diagnosis and treatment.
Complications related to surgery (e.g., infection, bleeding, scarring).
For breast CIS, potential for bilateral disease (LCIS 20-40%, DCIS 10-20%).

sections.p: Management of carcinoma in situ aims to remove the abnormal cells completely and prevent progression to invasive cancer. Treatment strategies are site-specific and depend on the extent and grade of the lesion.
b: Surgical excision is the primary treatment for most CIS, aiming for clear margins.
For DCIS, mastectomy is curative in 95% of cases; breast-conserving surgery with radiation is an alternative.
Cervical CIS may be treated with LEEP (Loop Electrosurgical Excision Procedure) or cone biopsy.
Topical therapies (e.g., imiquimod, 5-fluorouracil) may be used for some skin SCCIS.
Circumcision can treat Zoon's balanitis, which resembles CIS.
Regular follow-up is crucial to detect recurrence or new lesions.

sections.p: Long-term follow-up is essential to monitor for recurrence or the development of new lesions, especially given the risk of bilaterality in some forms of CIS. Prevention focuses on reducing exposure to known risk factors.
b: Regular clinical examinations and imaging (e.g., mammograms for breast CIS).
Cervical cytology and colposcopy for cervical CIS.
Sun protection and regular skin checks for skin SCCIS.
HPV vaccination to prevent cervical and anogenital CIS.
Smoking cessation to reduce risk of various cancers, including bronchial CIS.
Genetic counseling for individuals with strong family history of cancer.

sections.p: It is crucial to differentiate carcinoma in situ from benign conditions that mimic it, as well as from invasive carcinoma, which requires different management.
b: Invasive carcinoma: CIS is confined to the epithelium; invasive carcinoma has breached the basement membrane.
Dysplasia (low-grade): Dysplasia is less severe cellular atypia than CIS.
Paget disease of the nipple: This is an intraepithelial adenocarcinoma, often associated with underlying DCIS or invasive breast cancer, but distinct from other forms of CIS.
Zoon's balanitis: A benign inflammatory condition that clinically resembles SCCIS of the glans but is histologically distinct.
Lichen sclerosus: Can cause white, atrophic patches on genital skin, sometimes mistaken for SCCIS.

sections.p: Interpreting results requires careful consideration, as certain findings can be ambiguous or lead to misdiagnosis if not correlated with clinical context.
b: Inadequate biopsy: A superficial biopsy might miss an underlying invasive component.
Sampling error: Biopsy may miss the area of highest grade or invasion.
Inflammation: Can mimic cellular atypia, leading to false positives on cytology or biopsy.
Over-interpretation: Benign reactive changes can sometimes be mistaken for dysplasia or CIS.
False negatives: A normal Pap smear does not entirely rule out cervical CIS, especially if sampling was inadequate.

whenToSeekHelp: New or growing skin lesions that are red, scaly, or non-healing
Persistent abnormal vaginal bleeding or discharge
New breast lumps or changes, especially with nipple discharge or skin changes
Any persistent, unexplained lesion on the glans or prepuce

faq.q: Can carcinoma in situ spread to other parts of the body?
faq.a: No, by definition, carcinoma in situ is confined to the epithelial layer and has not invaded the basement membrane, so it cannot spread (metastasize) to other parts of the body.

faq.q: Is carcinoma in situ considered cancer?
faq.a: Yes, it is considered a very early, non-invasive form of cancer. It has the potential to become invasive cancer if left untreated, but at the CIS stage, it is not life-threatening in the same way invasive cancer is.

faq.q: What is the difference between DCIS and LCIS?
faq.a: Ductal Carcinoma In Situ (DCIS) is a direct precursor to invasive ductal carcinoma. Lobular Carcinoma In Situ (LCIS) is considered a marker of increased risk for developing invasive cancer in either breast, rather than a direct precursor.

exam: A 45-year-old uncircumcised man presents with a persistent, velvety red plaque on his glans. What is your initial differential diagnosis, and how would you confirm it in a low-resource setting? — Erythroplasia of Queyrat (SCCIS), Zoon's balanitis, candidiasis. Confirm with a punch biopsy, even if facilities are limited, as it's crucial to rule out SCCIS.

You receive a pathology report for a breast biopsy showing 'Ductal Carcinoma In Situ, high-grade, with comedo necrosis.' What is the immediate clinical implication for this patient, and what management options would you discuss? — High risk of progression to invasive cancer. Discuss mastectomy (curative in 95%) or breast-conserving surgery with adjuvant radiotherapy. Emphasize the need for clear margins.

A 30-year-old woman with HIV presents with an abnormal Pap smear showing HSIL. What is your next step, and why is HIV status particularly relevant here? — Colposcopy with directed biopsies. HIV-positive patients have a higher risk of persistent HPV infection, faster progression of CIN to CIS, and higher rates of recurrence after treatment.

Distinguish between carcinoma in situ and invasive carcinoma from a pathological perspective. Why is this distinction critical for patient prognosis and treatment? — CIS: abnormal cells confined to epithelium, intact basement membrane, no metastasis. Invasive: cells breach basement membrane, potential for metastasis. Critical because CIS is curable with local excision, while invasive cancer requires more aggressive systemic treatment and has a worse prognosis.

A patient with a diagnosis of Lobular Carcinoma In Situ (LCIS) asks if she needs a mastectomy. How would you counsel her regarding her risk and management? — LCIS is a risk marker, not a direct precursor. It indicates an increased risk (8-10 times) of developing invasive cancer in either breast. Discuss close surveillance, chemoprevention (e.g., tamoxifen), and bilateral prophylactic mastectomy as an option for very high-risk individuals, but not typically a primary treatment

What are the key preventive strategies for cervical carcinoma in situ, particularly relevant in East African settings? — HPV vaccination for young girls, regular cervical cancer screening (Pap smears or visual inspection with acetic acid - VIA), and prompt treatment of pre-cancerous lesions. Education on safe sexual practices and HIV prevention are also important.

A patient has a skin lesion diagnosed as Bowen's disease (SCCIS). What are the treatment options, and what follow-up is necessary? — Treatment options include surgical excision, cryotherapy, topical 5-fluorouracil or imiquimod, or photodynamic therapy. Follow-up involves regular skin checks to monitor for recurrence or new lesions, especially in sun-exposed areas, and patient education on sun protection.
